claims.text: Tungsten particles will receive a conformal WC interfacial coating 10–20 nm thick.
The WC coating will reduce thermal resistance at W/Cu interfaces.
Reducing W/Cu interfacial thermal resistance will increase the composite's overall thermal conductivity.
WC-coated W–Cu composites will retain mechanical durability relative to otherwise comparable uncoated composites.
WC-coated W–Cu composites will retain irradiation resistance relative to otherwise comparable uncoated composites.
The WC coating will be deposited by an optimized chemical vapor deposition process.
The proposed CVD step will be performed at approximately 900 °C before consolidation and sintering.
Uniform WC coverage is required to avoid brittleness and maintain strong interfacial bonding.
The intervention will produce a continuous nanoscale WC interlayer at W/Cu interfaces.
The WC interlayer will minimize interfacial defects.
The WC interlayer will minimize thermal-scattering sites at W/Cu interfaces.
The ultrathin WC coating will improve bonding between tungsten and copper.
The ultrathin WC coating will improve electron transmission between tungsten and copper.
Improved interfacial bonding and electron transmission will facilitate more efficient heat transfer.
The WC interlayer will act as a barrier to radiation-induced defect propagation.
Suppressing radiation-induced defect propagation will maintain mechanical integrity under irradiation.
Coating thickness outside 10–20 nm or nonuniform coverage could cause brittleness or interfacial defects.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant thermal-conductivity increase, or degradation of mechanical durability or irradiation resistance, will falsify the hypothesis.
